codex.worst_flaw: The pilot uses offline device timestamps to award credit and measure success without independently validating that they reliably distinguish pre-job safety checks from late entries.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no replayable event or policy versioning, no independent shadow validation, and a single coordinator as the only appeal path. It also never sets audit sample sizes or a feasible pilot sample size, so neither the payouts nor the two-week staggered comparison can be trusted at this scale.

holistic.reason: Union-co-designed, privacy-protective, crew-level paid-time reward with safety audit guardrails, staggered pilot and fix-first approach is credible, but a group-level reward may be diluted by free-riding, a 4-week reward period is short, and lasting change relies on the checklist being embedded in the job flow rather than on the reward itself.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch requires independently validating recorded job starts against actual starts because a delayed start record can make a late checklist qualify for a reward.

claude.worst_flaw: Crew-level paid-time-off milestones create peer pressure on individuals to log checklists, and the design never checks how that pressure affects morale or cooperation. Its weekly goals also never say how crews with few or uneven eligible jobs are treated fairly against a fixed 75% threshold.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with union buy-in, safety-hold protection, staggered rollout and clear pause triggers, but a one-paid-hour reward is small, the 75% crew threshold may feel hard or opaque, and lasting change depends on the workflow default and fixes rather than the incentive.

claude.worst_flaw: The design relies on existing safety spot checks to judge quality but never sets audit coverage, a review owner or a trigger threshold, so rushed checklists ticked just to hit the 80% reward goal could go undetected. It also has no replayable event history, no independent shadow validation of counts before payout, no fixed appeal deadline, no power or sample-size analysis for the paired-crew comparison, and no cost or harm decision criteria.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot sets checklist completion thresholds but gives no rule for how much improvement the reward must produce to justify its cost and any decline in safety-check quality.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, privacy protections, a fixed workflow before the reward, a staggered randomized rollout and clear stop rules make it approvable, though the small reward and reliance on dispatch data and spot checks leave some uncertainty about lasting effect.

claude.worst_flaw: The only check on rubber-stamp approvals and misused holds is after-the-fact defect triage, with no independent sampling of review depth. The design also has no appeal process or replayable event history, and it ignores case mix such as large PRs and small personal review loads.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward metric counts holds as timely answers without auditing whether the holds are justified or tracking how long authors remain blocked, so a group can hit 80% without reducing actionable review delays.

holistic.reason: It fixes the queue first, uses a small reward, keeps counts private and out of performance reviews, and plans a staggered comparison, which suits sceptical engineers. Against that, a one-hour reward is weak, the 80% bar needs close tracking, and the 8-hour clock and holds could be gamed.

codex.worst_flaw: Groups can earn the reward through superficial reviews or by prioritizing easy PRs because quality checks rely on disputes and incidents, with no routine sampling of credited reviews or check for complex PRs left waiting.

claude.worst_flaw: Quality protection relies on lagging incident reviews and disputes, with no proactive independent sampling of review depth, and the 80% group threshold has no handling for groups with few PRs, case mix or uneven load.

holistic.reason: Co-designed, team-level, low-stakes reward with workflow fixes, quality guardrails and a randomised test suits sceptical engineers and avoids the usual backfire traps, though the two-hour reward is modest, the six-week pilot is complex to explain, and lasting change depends on the retained routing and protected time rather than the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The 85% group goal ignores how much review work each reviewer actually gets, as well as PR size and case mix, so a few large or out-of-hours PRs can push a whole group under the bar. The two-group stagger with self-comparison also cannot separate the reward's effect from ordinary week-to-week change, and its sample size and costs are not defined in advance.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch is blocked because the design specifies no routine check that submitted reviews meet its usefulness standard before they count toward paid time off.

holistic.reason: Fair, privacy-respecting design that fixes bottlenecks first and avoids individual leaderboards, but a two-hour paid-time-off group reward is modest, the weekly team number is low-salience, and the 85% target and measurement upkeep carry some risk.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward score counts actions when urgent care or kiosk outages prevent timely logging, so following the safe fallback can cost the ward credit and pressure nurses to log within five minutes.

claude.worst_flaw: The core score depends on observers capturing a temporary staff code and matching it within a five-minute window, but the design never checks that this works in shadow mode first, so the kiosk logs could be paired with the wrong observed actions or miss them entirely, and nothing records versioned event and policy history to replay a disputed reward decision.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about safety, privacy, fairness and pausing, but it asks for a lot (matched audit, staggered rollout, a lead's weekly time, a 30-action minimum), and a shared catered meal is a weak incentive, so the habit may fade once the reward ends even with the one-tap workflow kept.

codex.worst_flaw: Monthly audits may yield no comparable observations during the two-week stagger, leaving the pilot unable to distinguish the meal’s effect from the workflow fixes.

claude.worst_flaw: The design pays a ward reward on kiosk-to-observation matching that it has not yet shown to be technically valid. It also has no independent shadow validation, event or policy versioning, or staffed appeal process beyond a single infection prevention lead.

holistic.reason: Careful design with safeguards (pause rules, pilot staging, no performance-review use, audit-based verification), but the matching logic is complex and depends on observers reliably pairing kiosk entries to observed moments, while the team meal is a modest, delayed reward and the logging habit may fade once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: Each audit session gives a very small n of observed actions, and the observer has to match a specific observed action to a single kiosk entry. Neither the matching method nor the observer burden is validated or shadow-tested, so the core measurement may be invalid. There is also no event log, no appeal process beyond the infection-prevention nurse, and observer presence could inflate logging during sampled sessions.

codex.worst_flaw: Reward launch should wait until the hospital validates that observers can reliably match each sampled hand-hygiene action to a single anonymous kiosk entry without changing when nurses log.

holistic.reason: Careful, safety-first design with verified outcomes, no individual scoring, and a pilot rollout check earns approval, but the observer-matching burden, team-meal reward that's easy to overlook, complexity of the explanation, and removal of reward tracking at week eight make durable behaviour change after the pilot only moderately likely.

codex.worst_flaw: The core measurement is a launch blocker because approved exceptions count toward both rewards and the sole success metric, allowing the programme to meet its target while useful article coverage stays flat.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never specifies a replayable event history, policy versioning or a staffed appeal path beyond messaging one ops lead. Combined with a decision threshold measured on a QA sample of unstated size and no protection against small-team inference in shared progress, the audit and decision basis is weaker than the rest of the plan.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, exceptions to protect quality, a staggered rollout to measure lift, and guardrails on CSAT and QA, but one paid hour for four weeks is a modest reward whose effect on habits after it ends is uncertain, though the default form change should help it stick.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout metric is misaligned with the programme’s goal because a team can qualify through valid no-article dispositions without increasing useful links or drafts.

claude.worst_flaw: The team reward counts 'No article needed' as a valid disposition, and only routine QA samples check those reasons. Agents can reach the 60% target by overusing that option, and the design sets no cap or trigger tied to the disposition mix (its pause rule covers QA pass rate and CSAT only). The design also leaves the weekly personal goal, small-team inference and eligibility denominators underspecified.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, team-level modest reward, quality guardrails, pause triggers, and a randomized stagger, but the one-hour PTO is a weak, delayed team incentive that may go unnoticed, and counting 'No article needed' as valid invites gaming even with QA checks.

codex.worst_flaw: Agents with enough tickets that warrant no article can earn the full reward through exception credits alone, even if they never link or write an article when one is warranted.

claude.worst_flaw: Everyone gets the same 60%/50% target and one tracker over the pilot, which ignores each agent's own baseline, small or uneven ticket volumes, agents with almost no eligible tickets, and leave or outages. Meanwhile, the 'No article needed' option is an easy way to finish fast, and only the existing QA sampling, at an unstated rate, checks it.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, no-penalty framing, quality checks, a CSAT pause rule and a staggered rollout, but a one-hour reward is small, tracker-only visibility may limit buzz, and gains are likely to fade once the reward ends beyond the workflow defaults.
